newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FEATURE - Australian coal miners battle for life.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Australian coal miners battle for life.

text.p: Australia's coal industry, the nation's biggest export earner, faces a battle for survival as mining companies hit by high costs, low prices and plummeting productivity, buckle under the pressure of global competition.
Some have put their operations up for sale after poor 1997/98 coal price contracts with their biggest market Japan and continuing struggles with local unions over wages.
"With the prospects we have in 1997, if we don't do anything different...profitability will disappear," the chairman of the New South Wales Minerals Council, Terry O'Reilly, told Reuters.

O'Reilly, who is also managing director of leading semi-soft coking coal producer Coal and Allied Industries Ltd, said lower cost structures together with higher productivity were vital for the survival of the Australian sector.
Industry executives constantly complain of falling productivity and see improvements here as the only real way to combat flat export prices.
All companies exporting coal to Japan were disappointed by the pricing round concluded in January, but hardest-hit were semi-soft coal producers in New South Wales state.

Semi-soft prices were cut by US$2 to $3 a tonne. Prices for quality hard coking coal, produced mainly in Queensland, stayed largely the same, while steaming coal prices were cut by $2.60 to $2.70 a tonne.
SALE RUMOURS 'PURE SPECULATION'

Poor returns and union difficulties have fuelled market speculation that Anglo-Australian miner RTZ-CRA might quit its Hunter Valley coal operations in New South Wales by selling its 71 percent stake in Coal and Allied.

U.S. miner Atlantic Richfield is already on the way out. It put its Arco Coal assets in Queensland state's Bowen Basin up for sale this month, while Exxon Corp has its New South Wales coal mining assets up for auction.

RTZ-CRA has described questions about the possible sale of its New South Wales coal operations as "pure speculation". But Coal and Allied's net profit in calendar 1996 fell to A$4.06 million ($3.16 million) from A$41.99 million the year before.
Chief executive Leon Davis told U.S. analysts that Coal and Allied mines were higher cost operations, but added:
"RTZ-CRA believes that strong Asian demand, broad micro-economic reforms and improved industrial relations augur well for its current and potential Australian coal operations."
COST OF COAL WORKERS
Analysts said RTZ-CRA, together with its counterparts in the Queensland coal industry, have been at the forefront of attempts to streamline industrial relations.
"Coal workers are paid well but no longer is there public support for the old unionism," Maree Klemm, an analyst with Brisbane broker Morgan Stockbroking Ltd, said.
Klemm said economies of scale were being sought by coal companies in an industry where pay levels of up to A$150,000 a year for some surface workers and up to A$100,000 a year for miners were common.
"It is going to be a make-or-break year for (coal industry) industrial relations," Klemm said.
A Melbourne coal analyst agreed, stating costs, not prices, were the only consideration for companies in the coal industry.
Attempts by producers to introduce enterprise wage agreements with coal mining unions were only the first stage of an impending struggle between owners and workers, he said.
Enterprise labour agreements are based on individual operations rather than across the whole industry.
"This year will be particularly tough. It would appear we are heading into uncharted industrial relations waters," the analyst said.
The exit of some industry players comes despite a bullish coal production outlook for Queensland, the country's biggest coal-producing state.
QUEENSLAND COAL PRODUCTION GROWING

By the year 2000, Queensland coal production is expected to grow to 150 million tonnes a year, boosting the value of exports over the A$4.2 billion achieved in the 1995/96 financial year (July-June), Queensland Department of Mines and Energy director-general Bob Day said.
This increase from the current 93.7 million tonnes means new players could be attracted to Queensland from home and abroad, analysts said.

Australia as a whole produced 192.3 million tonnes of coal in 1995/96, exporting 136.2 million tonnes. Total national exports were worth A$7.8 billion in 1995/96 with gold the second largest export earner at A$5.6 billion.
